html:
Gendun Chopel (1903 to 1951) was a Tibetan monk, scholar, poet and painter, often called the first modern Tibetan intellectual. Born in Amdo, in the northeast of the Tibetan world, he trained at Drepung, the great Gelug monastery near Lhasa, where he was known as a brilliant and provocative debater.

In 1934 he left for India with the Indian scholar Rahul Sankrityayan and spent twelve years in South Asia. He learned Sanskrit and English, travelled to Sri Lanka, helped George Roerich translate the Blue Annals, a Tibetan history, and wrote a guide to the Buddhist sites of India, a history of early Tibet drawing on old manuscripts from Dunhuang, and a frank treatise on sex.

He came home in 1946 with modern ideas, such as that the earth is round. Accused of links with a Tibetan reform party in India, he was jailed by the Lhasa government and came out broken. He died in 1951, in the months after the Chinese takeover of Tibet. His notes on Madhyamaka, the Buddhist "middle way" philosophy, are still argued over, and he is a hero to Tibetan modernisers inside Tibet and in exile. He came from the same Buddhist world as the 14th Dalai Lama, also from Amdo.
